318 landed at `bf17dac`.

## What shipped

| Layer | Change |
|-------|--------|
| Sentinel module | `src/020-sentinels.{h,c}` — kinds, detection, emit writers, $ref store, capability validation |
| Spec interface | `lang_spec_t` gains `sentinel_emit_mask` + `sentinel_reconstruct_mask` |
| Lua encoder | non-structural values (functions, userdata, threads) emit `$lang_opaque` via `luaL_ref` instead of erroring |
| Lua decoder | detects sentinels in `JSON_OBJECT`; reconstructs `$lang_opaque` (lua only), reads `$ref` from store, rejects `$function_pointer` with a clear message |
| Capability declarations | Lua = REF \| LANG_OPAQUE both ways; C = REF both ways; Bash = 0 |
| Unit tests | 7 in `tests/020-sentinels-test.c` covering all sentinel machinery |
| End-to-end fixture | `tests/maps/318-lang-opaque/` proves the Lua emit side end-to-end |
| Makefile | tests that dlopen specs now link 020-sentinels + 018-runtime-builtins + 017-box-id so the spec.so's symbol references resolve |

**Final tally: ~193 tests pass across all unit suites + 17 integration fixtures.**

## Documented limits (all in the issue file)

- `$function_pointer` end-to-end reconstruction needs the amendment's wrapper-binary subsystem — multi-session follow-on. Producer emits the shape; consumer rejects cleanly.
- Intra-Lua `$lang_opaque` round-trip needs a per-cell native flag (the per-edge flag fights back against the producer's actual JSON write).
- Compile-time wire validation using the capability masks is declared but not yet walked.
- $ref store is leak-per-run; refcount-driven release is a follow-on.
- C and Bash sentinel emit-side wiring is declared but not yet implemented in their encoders.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The most striking finding of this slice: **the sentinel mechanism works end-to-end on the emit side, but the reconstruction side hits a per-edge-vs-per-cell mismatch in the dual-ring slot design.** The producer wrote JSON (because of a cross-language sibling), but the consumer's slot's per-edge classification says "same-language native." Two-axis classification (per-edge for the *language* match, per-cell for the *actual* format written) is the deeper fix. The capability masks I added today are the right primitive; the consumer-side decode pathway is the missing wire.

The Makefile work was surprisingly important — every test binary that dlopens a spec needs to carry the symbols the spec.so calls back into. The pattern of "runner-owned symbols + spec.so plugins calling back via -rdynamic" works beautifully for the runner, but each test binary doing the same thing needs the same symbol inventory. Centralizing those into `SPEC_LOADER_DEPS` is the project-level fix.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

What's next? Remaining untracked issues are **247** (debug build + per-box stats lens) and **249** (tap input mode with radial ports). Both are editor-side. The deferred work pile is now substantial: Bash bindings (319e/246), `$function_pointer` wrapper-binary subsystem (318), per-cell native flag (318 sub-issue), exporter rewrite, box-kind refactor for create_box/connect.

=== strategems/commit-language-is-runtime-language.md ===
# Strategem — commit messages describe the runtime, not the issue

## The pattern

A commit message that uses scope-of-issue language ("these features
belong together," "this isn't done until both ship") gets re-read
later as architecture language ("these features are coupled," "these
two things are not independently deployable"). Future readers cannot
tell the difference between the two; they only see the commit text.
The lie compounds because no one re-reads issue files for archaeology
— they re-read `git log`.

Where this kept showing up: the 317 commit text said the C and Bash
bridges "live or die together," which was true about the *issue
contract* (issue 317 said every spec must implement both directions)
but false about the *architecture* (the C bridge ships independently
of the Bash bridge; each spec is its own .so dlopened in isolation;
adding a Python spec doesn't touch either of them). A future reader
looking at the log entry would conclude the system is more entangled
than it is, and might design around a coupling that doesn't exist.

=== strategems/contracts-must-fit-every-implementer.md ===
# Strategem — a contract must fit every implementer, not just the simplest

## The pattern

When designing a contract that several implementers will satisfy
(spec interfaces, abstract types, system protocols), check whether
the contract's assumptions hold for *every* class of implementer,
not just the cleanest case in front of you. A contract that works
for one class and almost-works for another is a contract that
forces the awkward class into shims, hacks, or special-cases. The
right move is to weaken the contract until it fits everyone
honestly.

The trap is subtle: the cleanest implementer often comes to mind
first when you're designing. C and Bash specs in this project both
treat values as bytes — their bridges write to and read from `dst`
buffers. The proposed amendment to issue 312 designed the
dispatch-side normalisation around this: "dispatch calls the
consumer spec's `json_to_native` with a buffer, gets native bytes
back, hands them to invoke." Clean, symmetric, byte-oriented.

=== strategems/redesigns-change-the-surface-too.md ===
# Strategem — when a redesign changes the nature, change the surface

## The pattern

When a redesign changes the *nature* of a thing (a task becomes
not-a-task, a coupling becomes independence, a push becomes a pull,
a synchronous call becomes async), the user-visible reports and the
tests must also change shape to reflect that. Carrying the old
surface forward looks like back-compat, but it's actually a quiet
refusal to commit to the new design.

The classic tell: a redesign ships, an existing test fails, and the
instinct is to add a small branch in the new code that makes the old
test pass. That branch is the lie. It says "the new model is the new
model, except in the report, where it pretends to be the old model so
your tests stay green."

tasks. The pool runner's `outputs:` report used to list every box's
captured output, with read boxes producing their value. The first

{
  "content":"# 319f — `create_box` and `connect` as language-agnostic box kinds\n\n## Status\ncomplete\n\n## Parent issue\nDesign-correction follow-on to 319d/319e. Per parent-issue\nreview feedback, the per-language wrappers added in 319d (Lua\nbinding) and 319e (C binding) are an architectural smell — they\nadd work per implementer rather than per primitive. The right\nshape for these primitives is **box kinds**, the same way `read`\nand `write` are language-agnostic kinds the runtime owns and\nevery language uses by wiring values in and out.\n\n## Current behavior\n\nTwo new box kinds, both language-agnostic, both implemented in\n`src/012-dispatch.c` (sibling to `do_write_box`):\n\n- **`kind: \"create_box\"`** — single input port named `spec`,\n  carrying the JSON box-schema text for the new box. The box's\n  output is the new box's id string. Implementation:\n  `do_create_box_box` reads the input, calls\n  `runtime_create_box` (the same C function the per-language\n  wrappers call), writes the id to the output buffer.\n\n- **`kind: \"connect\"`** — single input port named `connection`,\n  carrying one connection-entry JSON object. The box's output is\n  the literal `\"true\"`. Implementation: `do_connect_box` mirrors\n  `do_create_box_box`'s shape.\n\nThe dispatch's per-task TLS (set by `dispatch_action` in 319d)\nmakes `runtime_create_box` and `runtime_connect` reach the\nactive graph + slot store + spec registry without needing them\nthreaded through the new box-kind `do_*` signatures.\n\n## Why box kinds instead of per-language callbacks\n\nPer the strategem `strategems/contracts-must-fit-every-implementer.md`,\na contract that requires per-language wrappers is one the\nawkward implementer (Bash) can't satisfy without shims. The\nper-language wrappers from 319d/319e:\n\n- worked cleanly for Lua (registered as `soramech.create_box` /\n  `soramech.connect`)\n- worked cleanly for C (header alias macros over the runtime_*\n  symbols)\n- were genuinely hard for Bash (needs line-protocol extension\n  back to the runner — the gap that made 319e defer Bash)\n\nThe box-kind shape collapses all three cases: every language can\nwrite a value to an output wire; every language can consume a\nvalue from an input wire. Routing the value through a special\nbox kind that knows what to do is the universal mechanism. Bash\ngets self-construction for free now — its box function just\nwrites the spec string, no protocol extension needed.\n\n## Compatibility with the per-language wrappers\n\nThe Lua and C wrappers from 319d/319e are not removed. 641	/* {{{ push_routed() — branch picker over routing.kind, then push */
642	static int push_routed(dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, const box_t *b,
643	                       const void *out_bytes, int out_size)
644	{
645	    /* Read and write boxes don't carry a routing kind; their
646	     * output fans plain. Same for call boxes with no routing set
647	     * (treated as plain). */
648	    if (b->kind != BOX_CALL) return push_to_downstream(ctx, b, out_bytes, out_size);
649	
650	    switch (b->routing.kind) {
651	        case ROUTING_PLAIN:
652	            return push_to_downstream(ctx, b, out_bytes, out_size);
653	
654	        case ROUTING_COMPARATOR: {
655	            double v = parse_double(out_bytes, out_size);
656	            const char *branch =
657	                (v < b->routing.comparand) ? "lt" :
658	                (v > b->routing.comparand) ? "gt" : "eq";
659	            return push_branch(ctx, b, branch, out_bytes, out_size, 0) < 0 ? -1 : 0;
660	        }
661	
662	        case ROUTING_ITERATOR: {
663	            if (b->counter_slot_id < 0 || b->routing.n_outputs < 1) {
664	                /* No counter slot or zero outputs — fall back to plain. */
665	                return push_to_downstream(ctx, b, out_bytes, out_size);
666	            }
667	            /* The counter is both the branch selector AND the order
668	             * tag for the consumer slot (issue 304 cell-tagged
669	             * ordering). Tagged consumers serve pops by ascending
670	             * tag, so parallel iterator tasks land in invocation
671	             * order regardless of which worker finishes first. */
672	            uint32_t idx = slot_read_inc(ctx->slots, b->counter_slot_id,
673	                                         (uint32_t)b->routing.n_outputs);
674	            char branch[MAX_BRANCH_NAME];
675	            snprintf(branch, sizeof branch, "out_%u", idx);
676	            return push_branch(ctx, b, branch, out_bytes, out_size, idx) < 0 ? -1 : 0;
677	        }
678	
679	        case ROUTING_RANDOMIZER: {
680	            if (b->counter_slot_id < 0 || b->routing.n_outputs < 1) {
681	                return push_to_downstream(ctx, b, out_bytes, out_size);
682	            }
683	            /* Mix the monotonic counter so consecutive invocations
684	             * don't go to consecutive branches. xorshift32-style,
685	             * no crypto pretensions. */
686	            uint32_t i = slot_read_inc(ctx->slots, b->counter_slot_id, UINT32_MAX);
687	            uint32_t h = i;
688	            h ^= h >> 16; h *= 0x85ebca6bu;
689	            h ^= h >> 13; h *= 0xc2b2ae35u;
690	            h ^= h >> 16;
691	            uint32_t branch_idx = h % (uint32_t)b->routing.n_outputs;
692	            char branch[MAX_BRANCH_NAME];
693	            snprintf(branch, sizeof branch, "out_%u", branch_idx);
694	            /* Randomizer is also multi-spawn-aware; pass i as tag so
695	             * any downstream tagged slot still serves in order. */
696	            return push_branch(ctx, b, branch, out_bytes, out_size, i) < 0 ? -1 : 0;
697	        }
698	
699	        case ROUTING_WEIGHTED: {
700	            if (b->counter_slot_id < 0 || b->routing.n_outputs < 1 ||
701	                !b->routing.weights) {
702	                return push_to_downstream(ctx, b, out_bytes, out_size);
703	            }
704	            /* Cumulative-band lookup against a counter scaled to a
705	             * fixed precision. The last band absorbs floating-point
706	             * rounding so the bands sum to the whole range. */
707	            enum { WEIGHTED_PRECISION = 1000 };
708	            uint32_t i = slot_read_inc(ctx->slots, b->counter_slot_id,
709	                                       (uint32_t)WEIGHTED_PRECISION);
710	            double total = 0.0;
711	            for (int k = 0; k < b->routing.n_outputs; k++) {
712	                total += b->routing.weights[k];
713	            }
714	            if (total <= 0.0) {
715	                return push_to_downstream(ctx, b, out_bytes, out_size);
716	            }
717	            int branch_idx = b->routing.n_outputs - 1;
718	            double acc = 0.0;
719	            for (int k = 0; k < b->routing.n_outputs; k++) {
720	                acc += (b->routing.weights[k] / total) * WEIGHTED_PRECISION;
721	                if ((double)i < acc) { branch_idx = k; break; }
722	            }
723	            char branch[MAX_BRANCH_NAME];
724	            snprintf(branch, sizeof branch, "out_%d", branch_idx);
725	            return push_branch(ctx, b, branch, out_bytes, out_size, i) < 0 ? -1 : 0;
726	        }
727	
728	        case ROUTING_DISTRIBUTOR: {
729	            /* Argmin over downstream slot fill levels: pick the
730	             * output branch whose busiest consumer slot is least
731	             * loaded, so load spreads across the downstream stages.
732	             * For multi-consumer branches the branch's "load" is
733	             * the max fill across its consumers — the branch is
734	             * only as fast as its slowest stage. Ties resolve via
735	             * the counter slot so a steady stream still rotates
736	             * across equally-empty branches instead of always
737	             * picking the same low-index one. */
738	            if (b->counter_slot_id < 0 || b->routing.n_outputs < 1) {
739	                return push_to_downstream(ctx, b, out_bytes, out_size);
740	            }
741	            /* Read the counter once. Use it both as the rotation
742	             * offset (so ties between equally-loaded branches break
743	             * in round-robin order, not always toward index 0) AND
744	             * as the tag carried on the push (so downstream tagged
745	             * slots still serve in invocation order). */
746	            uint32_t tag = slot_read_inc(ctx->slots, b->counter_slot_id,
747	                                         UINT32_MAX);
748	            int best_branch  = -1;
749	            int32_t best_max = INT32_MAX;
750	            for (int step = 0; step < b->routing.n_outputs; step++) {
751	                int k = (int)(((uint32_t)step + tag) %
752	                              (uint32_t)b->routing.n_outputs);
753	                char want[MAX_BRANCH_NAME];
754	                snprintf(want, sizeof want, "out_%d", k);
755	                int32_t this_max = 0;
756	                int found_any = 0;
757	                for (int j = 0; j < b->n_connections; j++) {
758	                    const connection_t *c = &b->connections[j];
759	                    if (!c->from_branch ||
760	                        strcmp(c->from_branch, want) != 0) continue;
761	                    int dst = c->to_box_idx;
762	                    if (dst < 0) continue;
763	                    const box_t *db = graph_box(ctx->graph, dst);
764	                    int port = c->to_input_idx;
765	                    if (!db || port < 0 || port >= db->n_inputs ||
766	                        !db->input_slot_ids) continue;
767	                    int32_t fill = slot_fill_count(ctx->slots,
768	                                                   db->input_slot_ids[port]);
769	                    if (fill > this_max) this_max = fill;
770	                    found_any = 1;
771	                }
772	                if (!found_any) continue;
773	                if (this_max < best_max) {
774	                    best_max    = this_max;
775	                    best_branch = k;
776	                }
777	            }
778	            if (best_branch < 0) {
779	                /* No outgoing connection on any branch — falling
780	                 * back to plain still pushes nothing useful, but
781	                 * keeps the action's contract (return 0 means OK). */
782	                return push_to_downstream(ctx, b, out_bytes, out_size);
783	            }
784	            char branch[MAX_BRANCH_NAME];
785	            snprintf(branch, sizeof branch, "out_%d", best_branch);
786	            return push_branch(ctx, b, branch, out_bytes, out_size, tag) < 0
787	                       ? -1 : 0;
788	        }
789	
790	        default:
791	            /* Unknown routing kind — push plain as the safe default. */
792	            return push_to_downstream(ctx, b, out_bytes, out_size);
793	    }
794	}
795	/* }}} */
```

## Recap

Four pile items shipped this session:

| Commit | What |
|--------|------|
| `175b0f9` | **319f** — `create_box` / `connect` as language-agnostic box kinds (closes the per-language-wrapper architecture smell; Bash gets self-construction for free) |
| `a8e010d` | **exporter rewrite** — local Lua replacement (reads the right project, incremental, no CLAUDE.md spam, six well-defined verbosity levels into per-conversation directories) |
| `9421bfd` | **318a** — per-call `output_native` reaches `push_one_connection` (fixes intra-Lua `$lang_opaque` reconstruction; the consumer now correctly receives `doubled=42` instead of the silent-fallback `fn-type=nil`) |
| `295f967` | **wire validation** — graph loader walks cross-lang edges and warns on producer-emit / consumer-reconstruct mask gaps |

**18 integration tests + all unit suites pass.**

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The 318a fix is the most striking item — the original 318 closeout misdiagnosed the bug as "need per-cell native flag at read time." The actual cause was on the *write* side: the per-cell tag was already correct, but the push was putting cells in the wrong ring. One misdirected diagnosis sent us looking in the wrong layer; threading the per-call flag through the push chain (5 functions) turned out to be the actual fix. Worth remembering for future post-mortems: **a per-X symptom doesn't always mean a per-X structural fix**. Sometimes the per-X data already exists and the caller's choice is wrong.

The strategems file pointed cleanly at the box-kind refactor — `contracts-must-fit-every-implementer.md` made the per-language wrapper smell obvious in retrospect. Reading the strategems before the work paid off.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Remaining pile

- **#3** `$function_pointer` wrapper-binary subsystem — biggest remaining; multi-session per the amendment
- **#8** Refcount-driven `$ref` release (current is leak-per-run)
- **#9** Auto-init of specs for runtime-introduced languages
- **#10** Growable dispatch arrays (replace 4096-box headroom)
- **#11** Box-delete confirmation when ports have shims
- **Bash translate callback** (246) — bash server line protocol extension

Each is meaningful polish. Want to keep going on any of these, or pause here?

{
  "command":"git commit -m \"$(cat <<'EOF'\nscripts: exporter gains time-anchored mtime, readable slug filenames, tiered CLAUDE.md inclusion\n\nThree improvements to the local transcript exporter:\n\n(1) Each exported file's mtime is anchored to the conversation's\nLAST message timestamp; atime to the FIRST. File browsers and\nsort-by-mtime tools surface \"when this conversation last had\nactivity,\" not \"when the file was rendered.\" Birth time isn't\nsettable post-creation by standard tools and stays as the actual\nfile-create moment — documented in the script's header.\n\n(2) Filenames switch from <conv-id>.md to <slug>-<short-id>.md,\nwhere the slug is the first user message slugified (lowercased,\nnon-alnum collapsed to hyphens, capped at 40 chars) and short-id\nis the first 8 chars of the conversation UUID. Examples:\n  hi-can-we-do-306-and-307-5670858b.md\n  hi-can-you-initialize-a-project-here-the-2029ad16.md\nThe slug is the closest thing to a \"summarized name\" we can derive\nfrom the JSONL — there's no built-in title/summary field anywhere\nin the conversation data, including ~/.claude/sessions/ and\nhistory.jsonl. First-user-message text is the best signal.\n\n(3) Per-level CLAUDE.md and memory inclusion in the frontmatter:\n  v0..v2 — conversation metadata only\n  v3     — also project CLAUDE.md (DIR/CLAUDE.md if exists)\n  v4..v5 — also global CLAUDE.md (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) AND project\n           auto-memory files (~/.claude/projects/<id>/memory/)\nThe included content is read at export time, not from a per-\nconversation historical snapshot — Claude Code doesn't keep one,\nand the JSONL doesn't carry CLAUDE.md content. A note in the\nfrontmatter calls this out so readers don't assume what's shown\nis exactly what the conversation actually saw.\n\nIncremental check rewrite: the output's own mtime can no longer\nserve (it's deliberately anchored to the conversation's last\nmessage). Replaced with a small state file at\nllm-transcripts/.export-state — one line per conversation,\nstoring the source JSONL mtime at the moment of the last\nsuccessful render. Second-run skip works cleanly: 0 rendered,\n15 skipped after the first export.\n\nOld per-conversation files named <conv-id>.md are renamed to the\nnew slug-prefixed names (git detects the renames and preserves\nhistory). The May-8 leftover bundles at the top of llm-transcripts/\n(2029ad16-*-v0.md and friends) were already absent on disk; they\nget deleted from the index here.\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>\nEOF\n)\" 2>&1 | tail -5",
  "description":"Commit exporter v2"
}
```

## What shipped in this stretch

| Commit | What |
|--------|------|
| `a24fba4` | **Exporter v2** — time-anchored mtime/atime, slug-prefixed filenames, tiered CLAUDE.md+memory inclusion (v3 / v4+), state-file based incremental |
| `cd7cc54` | **Box-delete shim warning + lazy spec init** — inspector prompts on delete when ports have shims; dispatch lazy-inits per-worker spec handles for runtime-introduced languages (cross-lang `create_box` now works) |

**19 integration tests pass.**

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The exporter v2 had a subtle bug worth flagging: anchoring mtime to last-message-ts broke the existing incremental check because the output's mtime equalled the source's mtime (or even fell behind, when the source was touched after its last timestamped entry). The fix needed a state file — a small artifact whose only job is to remember "source's mtime at my last successful render," decoupled from any user-visible mtime semantics. Two different time concepts (display vs. dependency-tracking) needed two different storage locations.

The lazy spec init is interesting because it inverts the original filter's premise. The filter says "don't init what you won't use"; lazy init says "init when you actually need it, even if that's later." The two together — eager init for static, lazy init for dynamic — give the best of both worlds without forcing one model on every case.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

- **#3** `$function_pointer` wrapper-binary subsystem — biggest, multi-session
- **#8** Refcount-driven `$ref` release
- **#10** Growable dispatch arrays
- **Bash translate callback** (246)

  "new_string":"/* {{{ $ref store round-trip */\nstatic int test_ref_store(void)\n{\n    sentinel_ref_store_clear();\n    const char *payload = \"0123456789ABCDEF\";\n    int len = (int)strlen(payload);\n    uintptr_t p = sentinel_ref_alloc(payload, len);\n    ASSERT(p != 0);\n    int got_len = 0;\n    const void *got = sentinel_ref_lookup(p, &got_len);\n    ASSERT(got != NULL);\n    ASSERT(got_len == len);\n    ASSERT(memcmp(got, payload, (size_t)len) == 0);\n\n    /* Lookup with a wrong pointer returns NULL. */\n    int dummy = 0;\n    ASSERT(sentinel_ref_lookup(p + 1, &dummy) == NULL);\n\n    sentinel_ref_store_clear();\n    /* After clear, the pointer is no longer valid (and may be freed\n     * memory — we only assert lookup miss, not dereferencing). */\n    ASSERT(sentinel_ref_lookup(p, &dummy) == NULL);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ $ref refcount: dec to zero frees the chunk */\nstatic int test_ref_refcount_dec(void)\n{\n    sentinel_ref_store_clear();\n    uintptr_t p = sentinel_ref_alloc(\"hello\", 5);\n    ASSERT(p != 0);\n    int len = 0;\n    ASSERT(sentinel_ref_lookup(p, &len) != NULL);\n    ASSERT(len == 5);\n\n    /* Initial refcount is 1. A single dec brings it to 0 and the\n     * chunk is freed; lookup misses. */\n    sentinel_ref_dec(p);\n    ASSERT(sentinel_ref_lookup(p, &len) == NULL);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ $ref refcount: inc balances dec */\nstatic int test_ref_refcount_inc_dec(void)\n{\n    sentinel_ref_store_clear();\n    uintptr_t p = sentinel_ref_alloc(\"balanced\", 8);\n    ASSERT(p != 0);\n\n    /* refcount 1 → 3 via two incs. Two decs leaves it at 1; chunk\n     * still present. Third dec brings it to 0; chunk freed. */\n    sentinel_ref_inc(p);\n    sentinel_ref_inc(p);\n    sentinel_ref_dec(p);\n    sentinel_ref_dec(p);\n    int len = 0;\n    ASSERT(sentinel_ref_lookup(p, &len) != NULL);\n    ASSERT(len == 8);\n\n    sentinel_ref_dec(p);\n    ASSERT(sentinel_ref_lookup(p, &len) == NULL);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ $ref slot reuse — a freed slot is reused by the next alloc */\nstatic int test_ref_slot_reuse(void)\n{\n    sentinel_ref_store_clear();\n    uintptr_t p1 = sentinel_ref_alloc(\"aaa\", 3);\n    uintptr_t p2 = sentinel_ref_alloc(\"bbb\", 3);\n    ASSERT(p1 != 0 && p2 != 0 && p1 != p2);\n\n    /* Free p1. We can't\n     * assert the slot index directly through the public API, but\n     * we can assert that after freeing one and allocating one,\n     * lookups behave: p1 misses, p2 hits, p3 hits. */\n    sentinel_ref_dec(p1);\n    int len = 0;\n    ASSERT(sentinel_ref_lookup(p1, &len) == NULL);\n    ASSERT(sentinel_ref_lookup(p2, &len) != NULL);\n\n    uintptr_t p3 = sentinel_ref_alloc(\"ccc\", 3);\n    ASSERT(p3 != 0);\n    ASSERT(sentinel_ref_lookup(p3, &len) != NULL);\n    ASSERT(len == 3);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */",

150	 * graph via consumer pulls, observed in the consumers' outputs. */
151	static void print_outputs(const dispatch_ctx_t *ctx)
152	{
153	    if (!ctx->last_outputs) return;
154	    /* Iterate over the graph's current box count rather than
155	     * ctx->n_boxes — the latter includes 319d's runtime-headroom
156	     * slots for boxes that may have been created at runtime; the
157	     * graph's atomic count reflects the actual population. Skip
158	     * any NULL entries defensively in case of races. */
159	    int n = graph_n_boxes(ctx->graph);
160	    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
161	        const box_t *b = graph_box(ctx->graph, i);
162	        if (!b) continue;
163	        if (b->kind == BOX_READ) continue;
164	        const char *out = ctx->last_outputs[i];
165	        if (out) {
166	            fprintf(stderr, "  %s → %s\n", b->id, out);
167	        } else {
168	            fprintf(stderr, "  %s → (no output)\n", b->id);
169	        }

## Two pile items shipped

| Commit | What |
|--------|------|
| `830361d` | **#8 refcount $ref release** — `sentinel_ref_inc`/`dec` added, freed slots reused on next alloc, three new unit tests cover lifecycle. Process stays bounded over time when callers `dec` what they no longer need. |
| `aed1199` | **#10 growable dispatch arrays** — chunks-of-64 replace the flat 4096-box cap on per-box state (spawn guard + capture). New `dispatch_captured_output` accessor for read-only consumers; opaque-typed chunk array in the public ctx struct. |

**All 198 tests pass.**

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The dispatch chunked-append is the *third* time in this codebase this exact pattern has appeared — first the slot store (319b), then the graph box index (319d), now per-box dispatch state. Each time it's the same recipe: stable per-item storage + atomic count + mutex-protected top-level growth. There's a generalized "chunked-append container" abstraction lurking, but extracting it now would mean three callers that each use it slightly differently. Worth flagging if a fourth use appears, then extract.

The `dispatch_captured_output` accessor was the right call over exposing the chunk struct — even the test code, which used to touch internals freely, now goes through the same accessor as production. The opaque-pointer-in-public-struct trick is ugly but lets the chunk struct stay in `dispatch.c` private without breaking inclusion order.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

```
# 313 — Research: whole-program same-language compilation

## Status
in progress — Lua slice landed 2026-05-21 (compile-time
concatenation in `soramech-compile.sh`, runtime detection in the
Lua spec, end-to-end test). C and Bash merges are follow-ons.

## Concept

Instead of one box = one function call going through the dispatch
layer + slot store + spec invocation, **merge all same-language
boxes at compile time into a single translation unit** for that
language. Box-to-box transitions within a language region become
ordinary function calls — the optimizer can inline across them, the
language runtime stays warm, and the slot store and dispatch layer
don't run for those transitions at all. Only cross-language wires
retain the slot machinery.

For C: every C box becomes a function in one big `.c` file, with
the build emitting one `.so`. Wire endpoints become direct calls;
the optimizer inlines based on its usual heuristics.

For Lua: every Lua function gets pre-compiled into one bytecode
chunk loaded into one shared `lua_State` per worker. Wire
endpoints become direct `lua_pcall`s into that chunk — no JSON
encode/decode, no slot push/pop, no spec re-entry per call.

For Bash: probably no benefit — Bash is already process-per-call;
fusing scripts doesn't help much. Skip.

## Relationship to 312 — what stays, what thins

312 defines the **wire format**: dual-ring slots (native ring,
JSON ring, ordering ring) per input port, per-edge classification
at graph load, JSON-only-at-borders, native-otherwise. Every
value movement between boxes goes through this machinery.

This issue's merge thins the **spec invocation overhead** — the
dlsym + bridge + lua_pcall (or equivalent) that happens once
per box invocation. For boxes in the merged region, the dispatch
holds a direct pointer to the function inside the merged module
and calls it without going through the spec interface.

The slot machinery stays alive in the merged region. Why:
**boxes still run as separate thread-pool tasks**. A producer
on worker 0 and a consumer on worker 1 still need slots to hand
off the value across threads. The thread pool's parallelism
depends on tasks being scheduled independently; collapsing
same-language hops to synchronous function calls would defeat
the pool entirely. The merge wins on the per-call indirection
cost, not on the wire format.

So a box invocation inside the merged region looks like:

1. Worker picks up the task.
2. Dispatch reads inputs from the box's slots (same as 312 —
   dual-ring native side).
3. Dispatch jumps to the merged function directly (this is
   what 313 wins).
4. Function runs, returns a value.
...
runner produces — the merge is transparent.

Deferred to follow-on slices:

- **C merge.** Concatenating C source needs care with static
  vs. non-static functions, file-scoped declarations, and header
  inclusion. Plausible approach: wrap each box's source in an
  anonymous namespace-equivalent (C doesn't have namespaces, but
  static-by-default at file scope + unique mangled exposure of
  the box's entry function would do it). Real work; not done.
- **Bash merge.** Bash already runs one persistent subprocess
  per worker (issue 308's UDS-server model); the "merge" would
  source every box's `.sh` file into the same subprocess
  environment at server startup. Smaller surface than C; sized
  somewhere in between.
- **Inline-into-dispatch optimization.** This slice loads the
  merged module per worker but still goes through the spec's
  `lua_pcall` for every box invocation. The big optimization the
  issue body talks about — turning box-to-box transitions into
  direct function calls inside the merged module — needs
  dispatch-layer work that hasn't started. The current slice is
  the foundation: load-once-per-worker. The direct-call
  optimization rides on top.

## Open questions (for the research, not for now)

- Cross-language wires inside the merged region: the merged region
  still has cross-language outputs that exit to other regions. The
  spec interface still applies at those boundaries, so the merge is
  region-internal optimization, not a global rearchitecture.
- C ABI for inlined wrappers: with whole-program optimization the
  wrapper-per-box generation might collapse to nothing. If the
  optimizer can prove a wire endpoint is always called from the
  merged region with known types, it can skip the wrapper.
- Iterators-with-side-effects: an iterator self-rescheduling its
  own task is normally dispatch-layer machinery. Inside a merged
  region, it could become a `while` loop. Whether that's safe
  depends on whether other tasks are blocked on the iterator's
  output slots — which they shouldn't be in a same-language region,
  but the analysis has to confirm.
```

184	    /* SOCK_CLOEXEC atomically marks both fds close-on-exec at
185	     * creation. This matters because multiple worker threads
186	     * concurrently fork their own bash subprocesses; without
187	     * CLOEXEC, child A inherits child B's parent-side fd, the
188	     * bash on the other end never sees EOF when its real parent
189	     * exits, and we leak orphaned bash processes that hang on
190	     * read forever. */
191	    int sv[2];
192	    if (socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM | SOCK_CLOEXEC, 0, sv) != 0) return NULL;

194	    pid_t pid = fork();
195	    if (pid < 0) {
196	        close(sv[0]); close(sv[1]);
197	        return NULL;
198	    }

202	         * across exec. The original sv[1] (still CLOEXEC) closes

204	        close(sv[0]);

212

233	    if (h->fd >= 0) {

243	            if (r == h->pid) goto done;
244	            if (r < 0 && errno != EINTR) break;

| **Lua merged module** (2026-05-21) | `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` produces `__merged__.lua`; `langs/lua/spec.c` loads it once per worker | Single Lua-state load instead of per-file lazy `luaL_loadfile` |

## What stays open research

The big optimization the issue body originally talked about — **inline-into-dispatch direct calls**, turning box-to-box transitions inside a same-language region into direct function calls that bypass the spec interface entirely — is genuinely dispatch-layer work that hasn't started. Cost/benefit isn't compelling yet: nothing has profiled the remaining spec.invoke as a hot path. The 313 closeout text carries this forward as research; the issue file in `completed/` documents what to revisit and why.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
Both new slices today are **sidestep solutions, not actual merges**. The Lua merge was a real merge — one file per language per map. The C and Bash "merges" are really "move the cost out of the hot path" — C precompiles to many `.so` files (not one), Bash pre-sources (but each file stays its own source). The original 313 design wanted true source-level fusion; the practical answer is "you don't need fusion if you've already removed the per-call init cost."

This is the recurring pattern from earlier in the session: **a per-X symptom doesn't always mean a per-X structural fix**. 313 wanted to merge to eliminate spec invocation overhead; turns out eliminating *compile-time* and *source-time* overhead got most of the win without needing source-level merge at all.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Phase 3 is effectively at the closeout boundary — every numbered issue is either complete or moved to completed/, with the remaining items being deliberate open research (313's inline-into-dispatch, 318's `$function_pointer` wrapper-binary subsystem, 246's bash translate callback). # 248 — Encapsulated map as box

## Status
open

## Concept

A map directory is normally opened via the map-select UI as the
top-level graph being edited. **This issue adds a second way to
open a map:** through the file browser, as an *encapsulated box*
on the currently-edited parent map. The opened map becomes a
single box on the parent's canvas. Its inputs come from `data`
boxes inside the sub-map that have been marked
**externally-supplied**; its outputs come from `write` boxes
inside the sub-map that have been marked **externally-consumed**.
The two markings are symmetric: one redirects an input from "file
on disk" to "wire from parent," the other redirects an output
from "file on disk" to "wire to parent."

Encapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph.
The parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals; it sees one box
with declared input ports, declared output ports, and known
semantics. The sub-map can be edited independently, reused across
parent maps, and packaged once for distribution.

**Encapsulated boxes are the documented exception to issue 218's
"single output per box" rule.** Every other box kind has exactly
one output (with fan-out via multiple wires leaving that one
output). An encapsulated map has *N* distinct output ports, one
per `write` box marked externally-consumed. *N* may be zero (the
map is a pure side-effect sink), one (matches the common case),
or many. The exception exists because an encapsulated map's
outputs are independent values produced by independent
`write` boxes — packing them into a single blob (the earlier
design in this issue) would have repurposed file-writing
machinery to emit strings into wires, which is the wrong shape:
`write` boxes should keep their semantics ("terminate a value")
and the destination kind ("file vs. parent wire") should be a
mode toggle, not a substitution.

## Marked input ports inside the sub-map

A **data** box inside the sub-map (kind: `data`, the existing
language-agnostic file-IO source) can be marked as
**externally-supplied** via a small toggle on the box's
inspector. Toggling declares: "this data box's value comes from
the encapsulating context, not from its `path` or `value`
field."

The toggle is intentionally scoped to `data` boxes — those are
the natural entry points for external values into a map. Call
boxes / read boxes / write boxes don't carry the toggle, which
keeps the inspector uncluttered for the common cases. Each
external input becomes a small shared-memory chunk seeded by
the encapsulating call's invoke; the marked data box reads from
that chunk on each fire, treating it identically to a value
loaded from disk.

The toggle records the port's binding kind on the box JSON:

```json
{
    "id": "sum_input",
    "kind": "data",
    "external": {
        "kind": "named",            // or "positional" / "numbered"
        "name": "count",            // for named
        "index": 0                  // for positional / numbered
    },
    "...": "..."
}
```

Three binding kinds capture how the encapsulating box's input
maps to this internal port:

- **`positional`** — bound by argument order. The encapsulating
  box has N input ports; the *k*th port's value flows to the
  internal box whose `external.index` is *k*. Conceptually
  matches positional function arguments.
- **`numbered`** — bound by an explicit integer index. Same shape
  as positional but the user picks the number (so they can leave
  gaps, reorder freely, etc.).
- **`named`** — bound by a string name. The encapsulating box's
  input port has a label; the matching internal box's
  `external.name` is the same string.

A single sub-map can mix kinds across its marked boxes — some
positional, some named — and the parent map's encapsulated box
exposes the union as its input ports.

## Marked output ports inside the sub-map

A **write** box inside the sub-map (kind: `write`, issue 229's
file-write kind) can be marked as **externally-consumed** via a
small toggle on the box's inspector — the mirror of the
externally-supplied toggle on data boxes. Toggling declares:
"this write box's value goes to the encapsulating context, not
to its `path` field."

The toggle is intentionally scoped to `write` boxes — those are
the natural exit points for values out of a map. Each
externally-consumed write box surfaces as one **distinct output
port** on the encapsulating box. The port carries that one
value, on its own wire, to whichever downstream box(es) the
parent wires it to.

The toggle records the port's binding kind on the box JSON, in
the same shape as the input-side toggle:

```json
{
    "id": "result_value",
    "kind": "write",
    "external": {
        "kind": "named",            // or "positional" / "numbered"
        "name": "result",           // for named
        "index": 0                  // for positional / numbered
    },
    "...": "..."
```

```
## Suggested implementation sequence

1. **Box JSON schema**: add `kind: "map"`, the `ref` field, and
   the per-input `external` block. Graph loader rejects with a
   clear error if any field is missing where required.
2. **External-binding toggles**: inspector toggle on data boxes
   (externally-supplied) and write boxes (externally-consumed);
   kind / name / index selectors when on. Same visual idiom for
   both.
3. **File browser "Encapsulate" action**: adds a `kind: "map"`
   box to the parent at the cursor position. Reads the sub-map's
   marked data boxes and marked write boxes to populate the new
   box's `inputs` and `outputs` arrays.
4. **Graph loader sub-map resolution**: load the sub-map's
   `meta.json` and `boxes/`; record its marked-input and
   marked-output lists on the parent box record.
5. **Multi-output slot allocation**: the encapsulated box gets
   one output slot per externally-consumed write box (the
   documented exception to issue 218). Graph loader and slot
   store accept this shape only for `lang: "map"` boxes.
6. **Pick A or B**: compile-time inlining or runtime sub-graph
   dispatch. Prototype the simpler of the two end-to-end on a
   trivial sub-map (`maps/encap-trivial`).
7. **Recursion**: nested encapsulation; cycle detection at
   compile (or load) time.
8. **Editor visualization**: distinct canvas rendering for
   encapsulating boxes; tooltip / thumbnail.

## Open questions

- **Sub-map identity for the editor**: when the parent
  encapsulates `maps/<sub>`, what happens if the user later
  renames or moves `<sub>`? The reference path is brittle.
  Options: store a stable id in the sub-map's `meta.json` and
  reference that, plus a path hint; or require the sub-map to
  live inside the parent's map directory tree.
- **Re-sync behaviour when the sub-map changes**: if the user
  edits the sub-map and changes its marked inputs, the parent's
  encapsulating box's `inputs` array drifts out of date. Likely
  resolution: on parent map load, the loader re-derives the
  inputs from the sub-map and warns the user if wiring needs
  fixing.
- **`.map` packaging format**: this issue assumes sub-maps are
  directories. A single-file `.map` archive (tarball / zip)
  would be more portable for distribution. Out of scope here;
  separate ticket if it becomes relevant.
- **Output naming consistency**: outputs use the same
  positional / numbered / named binding kinds as inputs. The
  question is whether a single encapsulated box can mix kinds
  across outputs (e.g. two named, one positional), or whether
  all outputs must share a kind. Inputs already allow mixing —
  preferable to keep outputs symmetric.
- **Side-effect ordering**: the sub-map's write boxes run as
  part of the sub-graph and write to disk. The encapsulating
  box's output emits *after* those side effects complete. If
  the parent wires the encapsulating box's output forward, the
  downstream task can rely on the writes having happened. Worth
  documenting; not a design choice so much as a consequence of
  the existing dispatch model.

## Design history

The original 2026-05-21 design packed all write-box outputs into
a single byte-blob with a leading null-terminated size index, and
the encapsulated box had a single output wire carrying that blob:

> "the write data slots are the outputs, written to a chunk of
> heap memory. At the beginning is an array of sizes — null
> terminated. Then, immediately afterwards, is the first index
> of data..." — 2026-05-21

That design was reconsidered on 2026-05-23 while specifying the
self-construction built-ins (issue 319). The reconsideration:
boxes never "return" values to the outside world under the
existing model — they push values onto wires that other boxes
consume, and `write` boxes specifically terminate values to
files. Repurposing the file-writing destination to emit strings
into wires would have been a substitution of one mechanism for
another. The symmetric design — mark write boxes
externally-consumed, surface each as its own output port —
```

1	# 248 — Encapsulated map as box
2	
3	## Status
4	open
5	
6	## Concept
7	
8	A map directory is normally opened via the map-select UI as the
9	top-level graph being edited. **This issue adds a second way to
10	open a map:** through the file browser, as an *encapsulated box*
11	on the currently-edited parent map. The opened map becomes a
12	single box on the parent's canvas. Its inputs come from `data`
13	boxes inside the sub-map that have been marked
14	**externally-supplied**; its outputs come from `write` boxes
15	inside the sub-map that have been marked **externally-consumed**.
16	The two markings are symmetric: one redirects an input from "file
17	on disk" to "wire from parent," the other redirects an output
18	from "file on disk" to "wire to parent."
19	
20	Encapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph.
21	The parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals; it sees one box
22	with declared input ports, declared output ports, and known
23	semantics. The sub-map can be edited independently, reused across
24	parent maps, and packaged once for distribution.
25	
26	**Encapsulated boxes are the documented exception to issue 218's
27	"single output per box" rule.** Every other box kind has exactly
28	one output (with fan-out via multiple wires leaving that one
29	output). An encapsulated map has *N* distinct output ports, one
30	per `write` box marked externally-consumed. *N* may be zero (the
31	map is a pure side-effect sink), one (matches the common case),
32	or many. The exception exists because an encapsulated map's
33	outputs are independent values produced by independent
34	`write` boxes — packing them into a single blob (the earlier
35	design in this issue) would have repurposed file-writing
36	machinery to emit strings into wires, which is the wrong shape:
37	`write` boxes should keep their semantics ("terminate a value")
38	and the destination kind ("file vs. parent wire") should be a
39	mode toggle, not a substitution.
40	
41	## Marked input ports inside the sub-map
42	
43	A **data** box inside the sub-map (kind: `data`, the existing
44	language-agnostic file-IO source) can be marked as
45	**externally-supplied** via a small toggle on the box's
46	inspector. Toggling declares: "this data box's value comes from
47	the encapsulating context, not from its `path` or `value`
48	field."
49	
50	The toggle is intentionally scoped to `data` boxes — those are
51	the natural entry points for external values into a map. Call
52	boxes / read boxes / write boxes don't carry the toggle, which
53	keeps the inspector uncluttered for the common cases. Each
54	external input becomes a small shared-memory chunk seeded by
55	the encapsulating call's invoke; the marked data box reads from
56	that chunk on each fire, treating it identically to a value
57	loaded from disk.
58	
59	The toggle records the port's binding kind on the box JSON:
60	
61	```json
62	{
63	    "id": "sum_input",
64	    "kind": "data",
65	    "external": {
66	        "kind": "named",            // or "positional" / "numbered"
67	        "name": "count",            // for named
68	        "index": 0                  // for positional / numbered
69	    },
70	    "...": "..."
71	}
72	```
73	
74	Three binding kinds capture how the encapsulating box's input
75	maps to this internal port:
76	
77	- **`positional`** — bound by argument order. The encapsulating
78	  box has N input ports; the *k*th port's value flows to the
79	  internal box whose `external.index` is *k*. Conceptually
80	  matches positional function arguments.
81	- **`numbered`** — bound by an explicit integer index. Same shape
82	  as positional but the user picks the number (so they can leave
83	  gaps, reorder freely, etc.).
84	- **`named`** — bound by a string name. The encapsulating box's
85	  input port has a label; the matching internal box's
86	  `external.name` is the same string.
87	
88	A single sub-map can mix kinds across its marked boxes — some
89	positional, some named — and the parent map's encapsulated box
90	exposes the union as its input ports.
91	
92	## Marked output ports inside the sub-map
93	
94	A **write** box inside the sub-map (kind: `write`, issue 229's
95	file-write kind) can be marked as **externally-consumed** via a
96	small toggle on the box's inspector — the mirror of the
97	externally-supplied toggle on data boxes. Toggling declares:
98	"this write box's value goes to the encapsulating context, not
99	to its `path` field."
100	
101	The toggle is intentionally scoped to `write` boxes — those are
102	the natural exit points for values out of a map. Each
103	externally-consumed write box surfaces as one **distinct output
104	port** on the encapsulating box. The port carries that one
105	value, on its own wire, to whichever downstream box(es) the
106	parent wires it to.
107	
108	The toggle records the port's binding kind on the box JSON, in
109	the same shape as the input-side toggle:
110	
111	```json
112	{
113	    "id": "result_value",
114	    "kind": "write",
115	    "external": {
116	        "kind": "named",            // or "positional" / "numbered"
117	        "name": "result",           // for named
118	        "index": 0                  // for positional / numbered
119	    },
120	    "...": "..."
121	}
122	```
123	
124	Three binding kinds — same vocabulary as the input side:
125	
126	- **`positional`** — bound by argument order. The encapsulating
127	  box's *k*th output port is the externally-consumed write box
128	  whose `external.index` is *k*.
129	- **`numbered`** — bound by an explicit integer index, allowing
130	  gaps and reordering.
131	- **`named`** — bound by a string name. The encapsulating box's
132	  output port carries that label.
133	
134	A write box marked externally-consumed **also** writes to its
135	`path` if one is set — the two destinations are independent. The
136	write box can opt out of the file write (set `path: null`) if it
137	exists solely to surface a value to the parent.
138	
139	Each externally-consumed write box's emitted value becomes an
140	independent output wire on the encapsulating box. The earlier
141	design in this issue packed all write-box outputs into a single
142	byte-blob with a leading size index; that design is rejected —
143	see the "Concept" section for why. No packing, no unpacking
144	library; the wire format is the same per-port wire format every
145	other box uses.
146	
147	## File layout in the parent map
148	
149	**The encapsulating box is a normal `call` box.** From the
150	editor's perspective it has the same JSON shape as any other
151	call box — `kind: "call"`, `lang`, `ref`, `fn`, `inputs`,
152	`connections`, `routing`. What makes it an encapsulation is
153	that its `lang` is `map` and its `ref` points to a sub-map
154	directory rather than a source file. The map-language spec
155	(`langs/map/spec.so`) is responsible for the "behind the
156	scenes" processing — running the sub-graph and packing the
157	outputs.
158	
159	```json
160	{
161	    "id": "stats_pipeline",
162	    "kind": "call",
163	    "lang": "map",
164	    "ref": "../shared-maps/stats-pipeline",
165	    "fn": null,                                  // unused for map kind
166	    "inputs": [
167	        { "name": "count", "type": "int" },
168	        { "name": "label", "type": "string" }
169	    ],
170	    "outputs": [
171	        { "name": "mean",  "type": "float" },
172	        { "name": "stdev", "type": "float" },
173	        { "name": "n",     "type": "int" }
174	    ],
175	    "...": "..."
176	}
177	```
178	
179	The `outputs` array on the encapsulating box JSON is the
180	documented exception to the single-output-per-box rule. The
181	graph loader treats each entry as a distinct output slot,
182	allocates one ring buffer per output port (same machinery as
183	input slots, but on the producer side), and lets the parent
184	wire each output independently.
185	
186	The map-language spec is registered in the spec registry the
187	same way `lua` / `c` / `bash` are. Its `file_ext` is `.map`
188	(or no extension if the ref points to a directory). The graph
189	loader resolves the `ref`, the map spec's `init` (per worker)
190	loads the sub-graph, and its `invoke` runs the sub-graph and
191	packs the outputs. From the dispatch layer's view, an
192	encapsulating call is just another spec invocation.
193	
194	The sub-map's input ports (derived from its marked data boxes)
195	and output ports (derived from its marked write boxes) are
196	exposed on the encapsulating box's JSON as `inputs` and `outputs`
197	arrays. The user doesn't write either array themselves — the
198	editor generates them from the sub-map on first encapsulation
199	and re-syncs them when the sub-map changes.
200	
201	## Editor UI
202	
203	### File browser
204	
205	The file browser (issue 207's source-file-browser, or its
206	descendant) shows map directories with a distinct icon — a
207	folder-like glyph annotated to suggest "this is a runnable
208	graph, not a source file." Clicking opens a small menu:
209	
210	- **Edit this map** — switches the editor's active map (the
211	  existing map-select behaviour).
212	- **Encapsulate** — adds the map as a `kind: "map"` box to the
213	  currently-edited parent map. The new box appears on the
214	  canvas at the cursor position; the user wires it in like any
215	  other box.
216	
217	### External-binding toggle (inputs and outputs)
218	
219	The inspector for a `data` box's value-input grows a small
220	toggle that marks it externally-supplied; the inspector for a
221	`write` box's value-input grows the same toggle that marks it
222	externally-consumed. Both surface in the same visual idiom:
223	
224	```
225	  ┌─────────────────────────────┐
226	  │ count   [● external]        │ ← toggle on, port is externally-bound
227	  │   kind:    named            │
228	  │   name:    "count"          │
229	  └─────────────────────────────┘
230	```
231	
232	When the toggle is on, the inspector reveals the kind selector
233	(positional / numbered / named) and the name / index field.
234	When off, the port behaves normally (wires-in / literal value on
235	the data box; `path` write on the write box).
236	
237	A map with no marked data boxes encapsulates to a no-input box
238	(just a source of values). A map with no externally-consumed
239	write boxes encapsulates to a box with no output (side-effecting
240	only — legal but unusual; useful for "fire and forget"
241	sub-pipelines).
242	
243	### Visual on the canvas
244	
245	The encapsulating box renders distinctly — different border,
246	maybe a small "sub-map" badge — so the user sees at a glance
247	that this isn't a leaf call. Hovering shows the sub-map's name
248	and a small thumbnail of its graph.
249	
250	## Runtime model — two paths, needs a decision
251	
252	Two implementation paths exist. The encapsulating box being a
253	normal `call` box from the editor's perspective doesn't pick
254	between them; the choice lives in what the map-language spec
255	does behind the scenes and what (if anything) the compile
256	pipeline does at build time.
257	
258	### Path A — Compile-time inlining
259	
260	The compile pipeline (issue 309) recognizes encapsulating call
261	boxes and **expands them into their sub-graphs at build time**.
262	Steps the compile step takes per encapsulating box:
263	
264	1. Load the sub-map's graph from `ref`.
265	2. Rename every internal box with a parent-namespaced id:
266	   `stats_pipeline__compute`, `stats_pipeline__filter`, etc.
267	3. Copy every internal wire across, with the renamed ids.
268	4. For each marked data box inside the sub-map: replace it with
269	   a wire that brings the encapsulating box's matching input
270	   value directly to wherever the data box's output was wired.
271	5. For each externally-consumed write box inside the sub-map:
272	   route its emitted value to the matching output port on the
273	   encapsulating box (so downstream consumers in the parent map
274	   see the value on a distinct wire per write box). The write
275	   box still performs its disk-write if `path` is set.
276	6. Remove the encapsulating call box from the parent's graph.
277	
278	After expansion, the compiled artifact is **one flat graph**.
279	The runtime never sees `lang: "map"`. The map-language spec
280	exists only for the editor's sake (validating refs, listing
281	the sub-map's inputs/outputs for the inspector).
282	
283	**Pros:**
284	
285	- No new runtime machinery. The dispatch, slot store, and spec
286	  registry all operate on flat graphs as today.
287	- Best per-call performance — no sub-graph startup cost, no
288	  nested dispatch.
289	- **Composes cleanly with issue 313** (whole-program same-
290	  language merge). The inlined sub-graph's same-language regions
291	  merge into the parent's merge as if they were always one map.
292	- Debugging stack traces inside the inlined region point to
293	  flat box ids — readable once you know the naming convention.
294	
295	**Cons:**
296	
297	- The sub-map gets baked into every parent that uses it. Edit
298	  the sub-map → every parent must recompile.
299	- No hot-reload of sub-maps. The editor would have to
300	  re-expand on every parent map edit, or accept that the
301	  parent's last-compiled artifact lags the sub-map source.
302	- Compile time grows with sub-map size × number of
303	  encapsulations.
304	- Deep recursion (sub-maps inside sub-maps inside sub-maps)
305	  inflates the parent's compiled output proportionally.
306	- The multi-output exception to issue 218 has to be carried
307	  through compile-time inlining as well: after expansion, the
308	  parent's flat graph has wires going from internal sub-graph
309	  boxes directly to whichever parent consumers were wired to
310	  the encapsulating box's output ports. The compile-time
311	  artifact loses the "encapsulated box" identity entirely but
312	  preserves the per-output routing.
313	
314	### Path B — Runtime sub-graph dispatch
315	
316	The encapsulating box stays as one box in the parent's flat
317	graph. The map-language spec's `invoke` runs the sub-graph at
318	call time:
319	
320	1. **`map_init(worker_idx)`** — load every sub-map referenced
321	   by the running program (or lazily on first invoke). Each
322	   worker gets its own copy of the sub-graph state (slot store,
323	   dispatch context).
324	2. **`map_invoke(handle, sub_map_dir, ..., inputs, ..., outputs, ...)`** —
325	   for each input, write the bytes into the shared-memory chunk
326	   that the matching marked data box reads from. Then drive the
327	   sub-graph to quiescence using the existing pool's dispatch
328	   loop (the sub-graph's tasks are normal pool tasks distinguished
329	   by a nested namespace). When quiescent, walk each
330	   externally-consumed write box and push its emitted value onto
331	   the matching output port of the encapsulating box. Each output
332	   port surfaces on its own wire to the parent — no packing.
333	
334	The sub-graph's parallelism uses the same thread pool as the
335	parent's. A sub-graph's tasks compete for workers alongside the
336	parent's tasks. From the pool's perspective, the difference is
337	just box-id prefix.
338	
339	**Pros:**
340	
341	- Sub-map loaded once per worker, reused across many parent
342	  invocations and across many parent maps.
343	- Hot-reload friendly: change the sub-map, parent picks up the
344	  new version on next run (no parent recompile).
345	- The multi-output boundary is clean — each externally-consumed
346	  write box pushes onto its own output port wire as it would
347	  if it were a leaf box in the parent graph, no packing or
348	  unpacking required.
349	- Debugging stack traces preserve the sub-map identity (the
350	  task's namespace says "this came from `stats-pipeline`").
351	- Recursion is natural — the spec's invoke can nest-invoke its
352	  own spec for a sub-sub-map.
353	
354	**Cons:**
355	
356	- New runtime machinery: the map spec's `invoke` runs a nested
357	  dispatch loop. Either the dispatch layer grows a re-entrancy
358	  contract, or the map spec replicates enough of the dispatch
359	  machinery to drive the sub-graph itself.
360	- Each encapsulating-box call pays sub-graph startup cost —
361	  seeding inputs, possibly resetting slot state from a previous
362	  invocation, collecting outputs at the end. Small but real.
363	- Does NOT compose with issue 313's same-language merge — the
364	  sub-map's source can't merge with the parent's, because at
365	  build time they're separate compilation units. (313 could be
366	  extended to merge across encapsulation boundaries, but that's
367	  a separate design.)
368	- Re-using the sub-graph across invocations requires reset
369	  semantics. Either the sub-graph's slots and counters get
370	  reset between invocations (cost), or each invocation gets a
371	  fresh sub-graph instance (allocation cost).
372	
373	### What to weigh
374	
375	The choice turns on whether encapsulation is **a build-time
376	abstraction (like a C macro or a Lua-function-inlined-by-LuaJIT)**
377	or **a runtime composition (like calling a function in a shared
378	library)**.
379	
380	Path A treats it as a build-time abstraction. Encapsulation is
381	how the user organizes source; the compiled artifact is one
382	flat program. Best for raw performance and integration with
383	the existing machinery. Cost: rebuild propagation.
384	
385	Path B treats it as a runtime composition. Encapsulation is a
386	real boundary at execution time, with the packed-blob output
387	as the wire format across the boundary. Best for modularity,
388	hot-reload, and clear semantics. Cost: per-call overhead and
389	loss of cross-boundary optimization.
390	
391	A third option exists — **support both, picked per encapsulating
392	box** via a small flag in the box JSON (`encap_mode: "inline" |
393	"runtime"`). The compile pipeline expands inline-mode boxes;
394	runtime-mode boxes stay encapsulated. Each user picks per
395	encapsulation based on their needs. Higher implementation cost
396	but maximally flexible. Probably not in the first slice; flag it
397	for later if either A or B alone proves too narrow.
398	
399	Recursion (a sub-map encapsulates another sub-map) works under
400	either path. Cycles between maps are a compile-time (or
401	load-time, under B) error.
402	
403	## Relationship to existing issues
404	
405	- **Issue 207 (source-file-browser)** — the file browser is the
406	  entry point for the "encapsulate" action.
407	- **Issue 239 (literal port shrinks to nodule)** — the
408	  external-input slider reuses the same visual idiom on the
409	  input-port row.
410	- **Issue 229 (data box as language-agnostic file IO)** —
411	  encapsulation adds an "externally-supplied" toggle to data
412	  boxes and an "externally-consumed" toggle to write boxes. The
413	  boxes' default behaviour (read from / write to disk) is
414	  unchanged; the toggles route the value through a parent-wire
415	  instead of (or in addition to) the disk file.
416	
417	- **Issue 218 (single output per box)** — the encapsulated
418	  `kind: "map"` box is the documented exception. Every other box
419	  has exactly one output; an encapsulated box has one per
420	  externally-consumed write box (zero or more).
421	- **Issue 309 (build system / compile pipeline)** — the
422	  compile-time inlining path (option A above) extends the
423	  pipeline with an "encapsulation expansion" step.
424	- **Issue 313 (whole-program same-language merge)** — composes
425	  with compile-time inlining; the inlined sub-graph's same-
426	  language regions merge into the parent's merge as if they
427	  were always part of one map.
428	
429	## Relevant files
430	
431	- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box state, the `kind: "map"` box,
432	  the per-input-port external-binding state.
433	- `assets/js/005-app.js` — file browser; menu with Edit /
434	  Encapsulate actions.
435	- `assets/index.html` — inspector UI for the external-binding
436	  toggle.
437	- `src/006-server-main.lua` — HTTP backend; resolving sub-map
438	  paths, validating bindings.
439	- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — graph loader; recognise
440	  `kind: "map"`, resolve the sub-map, build the encapsulated
441	  shape.
442	- `src/012-dispatch.c` — encapsulating-box dispatch (runtime
443	  path) or compile-time expansion (compile path).
444	- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — encapsulation expansion if the
445	  compile-time path wins.
446	
447	## Suggested implementation sequence
448	
449	1. **Box JSON schema**: add `kind: "map"`, the `ref` field, and
450	   the per-input `external` block. Graph loader rejects with a
451	   clear error if any field is missing where required.
452	2. **External-binding toggles**: inspector toggle on data boxes
453	   (externally-supplied) and write boxes (externally-consumed);
454	   kind / name / index selectors when on. Same visual idiom for
455	   both.
456	3. **File browser "Encapsulate" action**: adds a `kind: "map"`
457	   box to the parent at the cursor position. Reads the sub-map's
458	   marked data boxes and marked write boxes to populate the new
459	   box's `inputs` and `outputs` arrays.
460	4. **Graph loader sub-map resolution**: load the sub-map's
461	   `meta.json` and `boxes/`; record its marked-input and
462	   marked-output lists on the parent box record.
463	5. **Multi-output slot allocation**: the encapsulated box gets
464	   one output slot per externally-consumed write box (the
465	   documented exception to issue 218). Graph loader and slot
466	   store accept this shape only for `lang: "map"` boxes.
467	6. **Pick A or B**: compile-time inlining or runtime sub-graph
468	   dispatch. Prototype the simpler of the two end-to-end on a
469	   trivial sub-map (`maps/encap-trivial`).
470	7. **Recursion**: nested encapsulation; cycle detection at
471	   compile (or load) time.
472	8. **Editor visualization**: distinct canvas rendering for
473	   encapsulating boxes; tooltip / thumbnail.
474	
475	## Open questions
476	
477	- **Sub-map identity for the editor**: when the parent
478	  encapsulates `maps/<sub>`, what happens if the user later
479	  renames or moves `<sub>`? The reference path is brittle.
480	  Options: store a stable id in the sub-map's `meta.json` and
481	  reference that, plus a path hint; or require the sub-map to
482	  live inside the parent's map directory tree.
483	- **Re-sync behaviour when the sub-map changes**: if the user
484	  edits the sub-map and changes its marked inputs, the parent's
485	  encapsulating box's `inputs` array drifts out of date. Likely
486	  resolution: on parent map load, the loader re-derives the
487	  inputs from the sub-map and warns the user if wiring needs
488	  fixing.
489	- **`.map` packaging format**: this issue assumes sub-maps are
490	  directories. A single-file `.map` archive (tarball / zip)
491	  would be more portable for distribution. Out of scope here;
492	  separate ticket if it becomes relevant.
493	- **Output naming consistency**: outputs use the same
494	  positional / numbered / named binding kinds as inputs. The
495	  question is whether a single encapsulated box can mix kinds
496	  across outputs (e.g. two named, one positional), or whether
497	  all outputs must share a kind. Inputs already allow mixing —
498	  preferable to keep outputs symmetric.
499	- **Side-effect ordering**: the sub-map's write boxes run as
500	  part of the sub-graph and write to disk. The encapsulating
501	  box's output emits *after* those side effects complete. If
502	  the parent wires the encapsulating box's output forward, the
503	  downstream task can rely on the writes having happened. Worth
504	  documenting; not a design choice so much as a consequence of
505	  the existing dispatch model.
506	
507	## Design history
508	
509	The original 2026-05-21 design packed all write-box outputs into
510	a single byte-blob with a leading null-terminated size index, and
511	the encapsulated box had a single output wire carrying that blob:
512	
513	> "the write data slots are the outputs, written to a chunk of
514	> heap memory. At the beginning is an array of sizes — null
515	> terminated. Then, immediately afterwards, is the first index
516	> of data..." — 2026-05-21
517	
518	That design was reconsidered on 2026-05-23 while specifying the
519	self-construction built-ins (issue 319). The reconsideration:
520	boxes never "return" values to the outside world under the
521	existing model — they push values onto wires that other boxes
522	consume, and `write` boxes specifically terminate values to
523	files. Repurposing the file-writing destination to emit strings
524	into wires would have been a substitution of one mechanism for
525	another. The symmetric design — mark write boxes
526	externally-consumed, surface each as its own output port —
527	preserves the `write` box's semantics ("terminate a value") and
528	treats the destination as a mode toggle. Cost: multi-output boxes
529	exist for this kind alone; benefit: one mechanism does both jobs
530	cleanly.
531	
```

123	static input_feeders_t scan_input_feeders(const struct graph *g,

876	/* {{{ cache_read_box_values() — issue 244
877	 *
878	 * Every BOX_READ's downstream value lives on its box record from
879	 * graph_load onward. Inline `value` literals are strdup'd; `path`
880	 * fields trigger a one-time file read whose bytes become the cache.
881	 * Once cached the read box never re-reads — its value is the run's
882	 * source of truth. */
883	static int cache_read_box_values(graph_t *g, char **err)
884	{
885	    for (int i = 0; i < g->n_boxes; i++) {
886	        box_t *b = g->boxes[i];
887	        if (b->kind != BOX_READ) continue;
888	
889	        if (b->value) {
890	            int n = (int)strlen(b->value);
891	            b->cached_value = malloc((size_t)n + 1);
892	            if (!b->cached_value) { *err = err_fmt("oom"); return -1; }
893	            memcpy(b->cached_value, b->value, (size_t)n);
894	            b->cached_value[n] = '\0';
895	            b->cached_size = n;
896	            continue;
897	        }
898	        if (!b->path) {
899	            /* No value, no path — error surfaces only if a consumer
900	             * actually tries to pull from this box, but flagging at
901	             * load is louder. Future iterations may allow `path`
902	             * inputs that arrive at run time; for now an unconfigured
903	             * read box is a load failure. */
904	            *err = err_fmt("read box '%s' has neither 'value' nor 'path'", b->id);
905	            return -1;
906	        }
907	
908	        /* Resolve `path` relative to the map directory and slurp the
909	         * file. The graph holds onto these bytes for the life of
910	         * the run. */
911	        const char *base = g->map_dir;
912	        size_t blen = base ? strlen(base) : 0;
913	        size_t plen = strlen(b->path);
914	        char *full = malloc(blen + 1 + plen + 1);
915	        if (!full) { *err = err_fmt("oom"); return -1; }
916	        if (b->path[0] == '/') {
917	            memcpy(full, b->path, plen + 1);
918	        } else if (blen > 0) {
919	            memcpy(full, base, blen);
920	            full[blen] = '/';
921	            memcpy(full + blen + 1, b->path, plen + 1);
922	        } else {
923	            memcpy(full, b->path, plen + 1);
924	        }
925	
926	        FILE *fp = fopen(full, "rb");
927	        if (!fp) {
928	            *err = err_fmt("read box '%s': cannot open '%s'", b->id, full);
929	            free(full);
930	            return -1;
931	        }
932	        free(full);
933	        fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_END);
934	        long len = ftell(fp);
935	        fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_SET);
936	        if (len < 0) {
937	            *err = err_fmt("read box '%s': ftell failed", b->id);
938	            fclose(fp);
939	            return -1;
940	        }
941	        b->cached_value = malloc((size_t)len + 1);
942	        if (!b->cached_value) {
943	            *err = err_fmt("oom");
944	            fclose(fp);
945	            return -1;
946	        }
947	        size_t got = fread(b->cached_value, 1, (size_t)len, fp);
948	        fclose(fp);
949	        b->cached_value[got] = '\0';
950	        b->cached_size = (int)got;

956	/* {{{ build_read_predecessor_lists() — issue 244
957	 *
958	 * For every call / write box, walk each input port and collect the
959	 * indices of any BOX_READ producers feeding it. The list lives on
960	 * the consumer's box record so dispatch can pull on demand without
961	 * a full graph scan. Reuses scan_input_feeders only indirectly —
962	 * we need the producer indices, not just counts, and the existing
963	 * helper doesn't expose them. The walk is small enough that an
964	 * inline loop is clearer than threading a callback through. */
965	static int build_read_predecessor_lists(graph_t *g, char **err)
966	{
967	    for (int i = 0; i < g->n_boxes; i++) {
968	        box_t *b = g->boxes[i];
969	        /* The kinds that run as tasks. BOX_CREATE_BOX and BOX_CONNECT
970	         * join the list with the box-kind path for runtime self-
971	         * construction (319 design-correction). BOX_READ never runs
972	         * as a task (it's pull-on-demand per issue 244). */
973	        if (b->kind != BOX_CALL && b->kind != BOX_WRITE &&
974	            b->kind != BOX_CREATE_BOX && b->kind != BOX_CONNECT) continue;
975	        if (b->n_inputs <= 0) continue;
976	
977	        b->n_read_predecessors    = calloc((size_t)b->n_inputs, sizeof(int));
978	        b->read_predecessor_ids   = calloc((size_t)b->n_inputs, sizeof(int *));
979	        b->read_pred_counter_slot = malloc((size_t)b->n_inputs * sizeof(int));
980	        if (!b->n_read_predecessors || !b->read_predecessor_ids ||
981	            !b->read_pred_counter_slot) {
982	            *err = err_fmt("oom");
983	            return -1;
984	        }
985	        for (int p = 0; p < b->n_inputs; p++) b->read_pred_counter_slot[p] = -1;
986	
987	        for (int port = 0; port < b->n_inputs; port++) {
988	            /* First pass: count. */
989	            int n = 0;
990	            for (int p = 0; p < g->n_boxes; p++) {
991	                const box_t *prod = g->boxes[p];
992	                if (prod->kind != BOX_READ) continue;
993	                for (int k = 0; k < prod->n_connections; k++) {
994	                    const connection_t *c = &prod->connections[k];
995	                    if (c->to_box_idx == i && c->to_input_idx == port) n++;
996	                }
997	            }
998	            if (n == 0) continue;
999	
1000	            int *ids = malloc((size_t)n * sizeof(int));
1001	            if (!ids) { *err = err_fmt("oom"); return -1; }
1002	
1003	            /* Second pass: fill. */
1004	            int idx = 0;
1005	            for (int p = 0; p < g->n_boxes; p++) {
1006	                const box_t *prod = g->boxes[p];
1007	                if (prod->kind != BOX_READ) continue;
1008	                for (int k = 0; k < prod->n_connections; k++) {
1009	                    const connection_t *c = &prod->connections[k];
1010	                    if (c->to_box_idx == i && c->to_input_idx == port) {
1011	                        ids[idx++] = p;
1012	                    }
1013	                }
1014	            }
1015	            b->n_read_predecessors[port]  = n;
```

end

-- {{{ M.sum_pair
-- Used by the slice-4 (issue 312) JSON-input test. Receives a
-- table parsed from JSON bytes and returns the sum of its two
-- fields. If invoke had instead handed us the raw bytes string,
-- the table indexing would error — that's the failure mode the
-- test verifies against.
function M.sum_pair(t)
    return tostring(t.a + t.b)
end

return M
